name: Diamond
fact: The hardest natural mineral, diamond is pure carbon crystallized over 150 km deep and carried up in kimberlite eruptions.
lore: Ancient Greeks called it adamas, 'unconquerable', and medieval tradition held that it gave its wearer courage in battle.
look: brilliant-cut colorless diamond with sharp fire and rainbow flashes

name: Gold
fact: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a translucent sheet about one square meter in area.
lore: In Inca tradition gold was called the 'sweat of the sun', and alchemists long chased it as the most perfect of metals.
look: raw golden native gold nugget, hammered texture with bright metallic luster

name: Painite
fact: Recognized in 1957, painite was long called the rarest gem mineral; only a few crystals were known until new Myanmar finds in the 2000s.
lore: With no ancient legends of its own, modern collectors treat painite as a token of rarity and of patience rewarded.
look: faceted cushion-cut painite gem, deep brownish-red with warm glow

name: Musgravite
fact: First described in 1967 from Australia's Musgrave Ranges, musgravite was not seen as a faceted gem until 1993.
lore: Too young for myth, it is cherished in collector circles as a talisman of the unexpected find.
look: faceted oval musgravite gem, soft grayish-violet with subtle sparkle

name: Red Beryl
fact: Gem red beryl comes almost solely from Utah's Wah Wah Mountains; its color comes from trace manganese, and crystals are tiny.
lore: Once sold as 'red emerald', it carries a modern crystal tradition as the beryl of passion and courage.
look: small faceted emerald-cut red beryl, vivid raspberry red

name: Grandidierite
fact: Named in 1902 for French explorer Alfred Grandidier, transparent gem-quality grandidierite was almost unknown until a 2014 find in Madagascar.
lore: In modern gem lore its sea-glass blue is linked to calm and clarity, a tradition only decades old.
look: faceted oval grandidierite gem, translucent blue-green like sea glass

name: Padparadscha Sapphire
color: Pinkish orange, like a sunset or lotus
fact: Its name comes from the Sinhalese word for the lotus blossom, and only a narrow blend of pink and orange earns it.
lore: Sri Lankan tradition likens its sunset hue to the sacred lotus, a symbol of purity and spiritual awakening.
look: faceted oval padparadscha sapphire, delicate pink-orange sunset color

name: Alexandrite
color: Green in daylight, red-purple in incandescent light
fact: Chromium makes it look green by daylight and raspberry red by candlelight; it was found in Russia's Urals in the 1830s.
lore: Legend says it was named for the future Tsar Alexander II, its red and green echoing imperial Russia's military colors.
look: faceted cushion-cut alexandrite, teal green shifting to raspberry red

name: Paraíba Tourmaline
fact: Found in Brazil's Paraíba state in the late 1980s, its neon glow comes from copper, an element rarely found in tourmaline.
lore: Modern gem lore calls it the stone of tropical lagoons, traditionally linked to calm, clear seas.
look: faceted oval Paraíba tourmaline, glowing neon turquoise blue

name: Ruby
color: Pinkish red to deep 'pigeon's blood' red
fact: Chromium gives ruby its red and a strong red fluorescence that makes the finest Burmese stones seem to glow from within.
lore: Sanskrit texts called it ratnaraj, 'king of gems', and Burmese warriors are said to have set rubies under their skin for invincibility.
look: faceted cushion-cut ruby, deep pigeon's-blood red with glowing fluorescence

name: Jadeite
color: Emerald green; also lavender, white, black
fact: Interlocking pyroxene crystals make jadeite remarkably tough; vivid 'imperial' green jadeite is among the costliest gems on Earth.
lore: Chinese tradition has long prized jade as the stone of heaven, a symbol of virtue, purity and long life.
look: polished imperial-green jadeite cabochon, glassy translucent emerald green

name: Benitoite
fact: Gem benitoite comes almost only from one California mine; it glows bright blue under shortwave UV and is California's state gem.
lore: Collector tradition holds it a lucky stone, since a single source makes every crystal a fortunate find.
look: faceted trilliant benitoite, vivid sapphire blue with strong fire

name: Black Opal
color: Dark body with flashing rainbow play-of-color
fact: Black opal's dark body tone makes its play-of-color blaze, and Lightning Ridge in Australia is its classic source.
lore: A widely retold Aboriginal Australian legend says opals formed where a rainbow touched the earth.
look: polished black opal cabochon with blazing red, green and blue harlequin fire

name: Emerald
fact: Most emeralds hold inclusions that gem traders call jardin, French for 'garden'; chromium and vanadium give their green.
lore: Romans held emerald restful to tired eyes, and the emperor Nero is said to have watched gladiators through one.
look: emerald-cut green emerald, deep velvety green with soft garden inclusions

name: Blue Sapphire
fact: Iron and titanium traces give sapphire its blue; corundum in every color except red is called sapphire.
lore: Medieval clergy wore sapphires as a symbol of heaven, and kings believed they guarded against envy and harm.
look: faceted oval blue sapphire, velvety cornflower blue

name: Demantoid Garnet
color: Vivid grass green to yellowish green
fact: Its dispersion exceeds diamond's, and Russian stones often hold golden 'horsetail' inclusions of chrysotile.
lore: Old garnet lore held that travelers carrying one were protected on the road, a belief jewelers extended to this rare green.
look: round brilliant demantoid garnet, grass green with diamond-like fire

name: Star Sapphire
color: Grey-blue to blue with a six-rayed star
fact: Fine rutile needles inside the crystal reflect light into a six-rayed star that glides across the domed cabochon.
lore: Sri Lankan travelers traditionally carried star sapphires as guiding stones, reading the crossing rays as faith, hope and destiny.
look: domed blue star sapphire cabochon with sharp six-rayed star

name: Pearl
formula: Organic: aragonite (CaCO₃) layers bound by conchiolin
fact: Natural pearls form when a mollusk coats an irritant in nacre; before cultured pearls, the Persian Gulf supplied the finest.
lore: Old legends from many lands describe pearls as tears of the moon or drops of dew caught by shellfish.
look: single round natural pearl, creamy white with soft rosy orient

name: Tanzanite
fact: Found in 1967 in a few square kilometers near Mount Kilimanjaro, most tanzanite is gently heated to bring out its blue-violet.
lore: A modern East African gift tradition presents tanzanite at a child's birth as a token of new beginnings.
look: faceted trillion tanzanite, rich violet-blue with purple flashes

name: Platinum
fact: Spanish colonists in Colombia called it platina, 'little silver', and once dismissed it as a nuisance in their gold washings.
lore: In modern jewelry tradition, platinum's endurance made it the classic symbol of lasting love and commitment.
look: raw native platinum nugget, silvery grey with rounded water-worn surface

name: Haüyne
fact: Haüyne crystals from Germany's volcanic Eifel are tiny; faceted stones over one carat are extraordinarily rare.
lore: Crystal enthusiasts traditionally link its volcanic blue with clear expression, much like its cousin lapis.
look: tiny faceted round haüyne gem, intense electric blue

name: Imperial Topaz
fact: Topaz has perfect cleavage, so one sharp knock can split even a flawless crystal cleanly in two.
lore: Legend says the name 'imperial' honored royalty, whether Russia's tsars or Brazil's emperor Dom Pedro II.
look: faceted pear-shaped imperial topaz, glowing golden-peach orange

name: Jeremejevite
fact: First found in Siberia in 1883, its best gem crystals came much later from Namibia's Erongo Mountains as slim blue prisms.
lore: Lacking ancient legend, it is prized among collectors as an emblem of rare and clear-sighted taste.
look: slender pale blue jeremejevite prism crystal, glassy and clear

name: Pezzottaite
fact: Identified in 2003, this cesium-rich cousin of beryl was first sold in Madagascar as 'raspberyl' or red beryl.
lore: So new that its lore is still being written, collectors keep it as a keepsake of a modern discovery.
look: faceted oval pezzottaite, raspberry pink with soft sparkle

name: Pink Sapphire
fact: Pink sapphire is colored by the same chromium as ruby, and labs still debate where pink ends and red begins.
lore: In modern gem tradition, pink sapphire is a stone of compassion and a favored alternative engagement gem.
look: faceted cushion pink sapphire, bright hot pink sparkle

name: Cat's Eye Chrysoberyl
color: Honey yellow to greenish with a sharp silky eye
fact: Parallel silk needles create a sharp line of light; gemologists reserve the unqualified name 'cat's eye' for chrysoberyl.
lore: In Sri Lankan and Indian tradition it was worn to ward off evil, and Vedic astrology links it to the shadow planet Ketu.
look: domed honey-yellow chrysoberyl cabochon with sharp silver cat's-eye line

name: Spinel
fact: The 'Black Prince's Ruby' in Britain's Imperial State Crown is actually a large red spinel.
lore: Medieval lapidaries, unaware it differed from ruby, prized red 'balas' stones from Badakhshan as royal talismans.
look: faceted octagon red spinel, vivid crimson with bright luster

name: Tsavorite Garnet
fact: Discovered in East Africa in the late 1960s, it was named by Tiffany & Co. after Kenya's Tsavo National Park.
lore: Modern gem lore links its fresh green to vitality and growth, echoing the savanna that lent it its name.
look: round brilliant tsavorite garnet, vivid emerald green with brilliance

name: Aquamarine
fact: Iron gives aquamarine its blue; a Brazilian crystal found in 1910 weighed about 110 kg, one of the largest gem crystals known.
lore: Sailors traditionally carried aquamarine, Latin for 'sea water', as a charm for calm seas and safe voyages.
look: emerald-cut aquamarine, clear pale sea blue

name: Clinohumite
fact: Gem clinohumite was virtually unknown until a 1983 find in the Pamir Mountains, later joined by Siberia and Tanzania.
lore: Modern crystal lore, with no old tales to draw on, ties its fiery orange to motivation and courage.
look: faceted cushion clinohumite, glowing tangerine orange

name: Sapphirine
fact: Named for its sapphire-like blue, it is unrelated to corundum and forms in very high-temperature metamorphic rocks.
lore: Among gem collectors it is traditionally offered as a quiet rarity, a stone for those who know where to look.
look: faceted oval sapphirine, soft violet-blue

name: Yellow Sapphire
fact: Traces of iron give yellow sapphire its color, and Sri Lanka has yielded fine canary stones for centuries.
lore: In Vedic astrology tradition, yellow sapphire (pukhraj) is the gem of Jupiter, worn for wisdom and prosperity.
look: faceted oval yellow sapphire, bright canary yellow

name: Boulder Opal
color: Rainbow opal veins in brown ironstone
fact: Boulder opal forms in cracks of ironstone concretions, so it is cut with the brown host rock left as a natural backing.
lore: Victorian superstition branded opals unlucky after a Walter Scott novel, a belief Queen Victoria herself ignored.
look: freeform boulder opal, electric blue-green opal veins in brown ironstone

name: Euclase
color: Colorless, pale blue to sea green
fact: Its name means 'easily broken' in Greek, a nod to perfect cleavage that makes faceting it a real challenge.
lore: Collector tradition treats euclase as a lesson in gentleness, its fragile cleavage a reminder to handle beauty with care.
look: faceted pale sea-blue euclase, crisp glassy facets

name: Opal
color: White to light body with rainbow play-of-color
fact: Play-of-color comes from stacked silica spheres that diffract light like a natural grating.
lore: The Roman writer Pliny praised opal for holding the colors of all gems, and Roman tradition made it a token of hope.
look: oval white opal cabochon with flashing rainbow play-of-color

name: Rubellite Tourmaline
fact: The 'Caesar's Ruby' pendant in Russia's old royal treasure is in fact rubellite; manganese gives the red.
lore: Crystal lore says rubellite opens the heart and kindles devotion, a stone of warmth in modern tradition.
look: faceted oval rubellite tourmaline, raspberry red

name: Sinhalite
fact: Long mistaken for brown peridot, sinhalite was recognized as a new mineral in 1952 and named after Sri Lanka.
lore: Named from Sinhala, Sri Lanka's old name, it shares the island's long tradition of gems carried as talismans.
look: faceted oval sinhalite, warm honey-brown with golden glints

name: Ammolite
color: Iridescent red, green, gold and blue
fact: Cut from ammonite shells about 70 million years old, gem ammolite comes almost only from Alberta's Bearpaw Formation.
lore: In Blackfoot tradition, ammonite fossils called iniskim, 'buffalo stones', were kept to call the herds.
look: polished ammolite slab, fiery red-green iridescent mosaic

name: Fire Opal
color: Yellow, orange to red, sometimes with play-of-color
fact: Unlike most opal, its glowing body color is the main attraction; many Mexican fire opals show no play-of-color at all.
lore: Crystal folklore says fire opal kindles passion and creativity, like a flame held in stone.
look: faceted oval Mexican fire opal, translucent glowing orange-red

name: Hiddenite
fact: Named for William Hidden, who found it in North Carolina in 1879 while searching for platinum for Thomas Edison.
lore: Crystal tradition pairs hiddenite with its pink sibling kunzite, calling the green one a stone of fresh starts.
look: faceted emerald-cut hiddenite, pale mint green

name: Indicolite Tourmaline
fact: Pure blue tourmaline is rare; indicolite is so pleochroic that it can look nearly black viewed down the crystal's length.
lore: Crystal enthusiasts traditionally pair indicolite with calm speech and quiet intuition.
look: faceted oval indicolite tourmaline, deep teal blue

name: Morganite
fact: Named in 1911 for banker J.P. Morgan, morganite owes its blush pink to traces of manganese.
lore: Modern crystal tradition calls morganite a stone of tender love and gentle compassion.
look: faceted cushion morganite, soft peach-pink

name: Phenakite
fact: Its name, Greek for 'deceiver', comes from being mistaken for quartz, though it is harder and far rarer.
lore: Some modern crystal circles regard phenakite as a high-energy stone, a recent tradition without ancient roots.
look: colorless phenakite crystal, sharp glassy rhombohedral faces

name: Spessartine Garnet
fact: Named for Germany's Spessart region, it became famous when vivid 'mandarin' garnets were found in Namibia in 1991.
lore: Medieval garnet lore held that a glowing garnet would darken to warn its wearer of coming danger.
look: round brilliant spessartine garnet, vivid mandarin orange

name: Tugtupite
color: Pink to crimson, deepening in sunlight
fact: Tugtupite is tenebrescent: it deepens from pale pink to crimson in light, then slowly fades again in darkness.
lore: A retold Greenlandic legend calls it 'reindeer blood' and says it glows brighter when lovers think of each other.
look: polished tugtupite cabochon, mottled raspberry pink and white

name: Color-Change Garnet
color: Blue-green in daylight to purple-red in warm light
fact: Traces of vanadium and chromium let some pyrope–spessartine garnets shift color; Madagascar's Bekily stones even turn blue.
lore: Crystal tradition sees color-change gems as symbols of adaptability, their shifting hues mirroring life's changes.
look: faceted round color-change garnet, teal shifting to purple-red

name: Diaspore
color: Kiwi green to pinkish champagne, shifting with light
fact: Gem diaspore from Turkey's Anatolian mountains changes from green in daylight to pinkish champagne under warm light.
lore: Sold under trade names honoring Ottoman sultans, it carries a modern tradition as a stone of transformation.
look: faceted cushion diaspore, kiwi green blending to champagne pink

name: Kornerupine
fact: Named for Danish geologist Andreas Kornerup and first found in Greenland, gem kornerupine flashes green and brown.
lore: A collector's stone with little folklore, it is traditionally gifted among gem lovers as a token of hidden depth.
look: faceted oval kornerupine, mossy green with brown flashes

name: Red Coral
fact: Precious coral is the branching skeleton of tiny colonial animals; Mediterranean red coral grows very slowly.
lore: Romans hung coral on children's cradles for protection, and Italian folk tradition still uses coral horns as charms.
look: polished red coral branch, glossy deep red

name: Titanite
fact: Also called sphene, titanite has more fire than diamond but is soft enough to scratch easily.
lore: From sphene, Greek for 'wedge', comes a crystal tradition tying it to sharp, clear thinking.
look: faceted oval titanite, yellow-green with intense rainbow fire

name: Watermelon Tourmaline
fact: Shifting fluid chemistry as the crystal grew left a pink core and green rim, best seen in slices across the prism.
lore: Crystal folklore calls watermelon tourmaline a stone of balance, joining heart-pink with nature-green.
look: polished watermelon tourmaline slice, pink center ringed with green

name: Zircon
fact: Zircon grains from Western Australia's Jack Hills are about 4.4 billion years old, the oldest known pieces of Earth.
lore: Medieval tradition held that zircon aided restful sleep and brought honor and wisdom to its wearer.
look: round brilliant blue zircon, electric blue with strong fire

name: Cassiterite
fact: The main ore of tin, cassiterite also has more fire than diamond, though clean gem crystals are rare.
lore: Ancient tradition placed the Cassiterides, the fabled 'tin islands', somewhere off Europe's Atlantic coast.
look: faceted cassiterite gem, honey brown with strong fire

name: Gem Silica
fact: Chalcedony saturated with copper-bearing chrysocolla, gem silica is far harder and rarer than chrysocolla itself.
lore: Crystal circles traditionally call it a stone of calm, peaceful communication.
look: translucent gem silica cabochon, glowing electric blue-green

name: Kunzite
fact: Named for Tiffany gemologist George F. Kunz, kunzite's pink can fade with long exposure to strong sunlight.
lore: Crystal tradition calls kunzite a stone of gentle love, and many wear it close to the heart.
look: faceted emerald-cut kunzite, soft lilac pink

name: Peridot
fact: Peridot forms deep in Earth's mantle and has even been found in meteorites; Egypt's Zabargad Island was mined for millennia.
lore: Ancient Egyptians are said to have called it the 'gem of the sun', hunting it on Zabargad by night when it glowed.
look: faceted oval peridot, bright lime green

name: Turquoise
color: Sky blue to green, often with matrix veins
fact: Turquoise has been mined near Nishapur, Iran, for over 2,000 years; copper gives the blue and iron pushes it green.
lore: Navajo and other Southwestern traditions treasure turquoise as a protective stone tied to sky and water.
look: polished turquoise cabochon, robin's-egg blue with fine brown matrix web

name: Axinite
fact: Its name, from the Greek for 'axe', describes the wedge-shaped crystals with knife-sharp edges.
lore: Crystal tradition links axinite's blade-like crystals to grounding and steady focus.
look: sharp wedge-shaped axinite crystal, glossy clove brown

name: Chrome Tourmaline
fact: Found in East Africa in the 1960s, its rich green comes from chromium and vanadium rather than iron.
lore: Tourmaline's name is said to come from the Sinhalese 'turmali', for mixed gem gravels, giving it a many-colored mystique.
look: faceted oval chrome tourmaline, intense emerald green

name: Green Tourmaline
fact: Dutch traders called warmed tourmaline 'aschentrekker' because its pyroelectric charge pulled ash from their pipes.
lore: Folk tradition names green tourmaline a stone of growth, said to bring luck to gardeners.
look: faceted emerald-cut green tourmaline, deep forest green

name: Heliodor
fact: Iron gives golden beryl its color, and its name comes from the Greek for 'gift of the sun'.
lore: That sunny name inspired a crystal tradition linking heliodor to warmth, confidence and willpower.
look: faceted emerald-cut heliodor, clear golden yellow

name: Lapis Lazuli
color: Deep royal blue with golden pyrite flecks
fact: Mined in Afghanistan for over 6,000 years, lapis was ground into ultramarine, once a pigment costlier than gold.
lore: Ancient Egyptians held lapis to be a stone of the heavens, inlaying it in Tutankhamun's golden mask.
look: polished lapis lazuli cabochon, deep royal blue with gold pyrite flecks

name: Nephrite Jade
fact: Felted amphibole fibers make nephrite one of the toughest gem materials; China has carved it for over 7,000 years.
lore: Māori tradition treasures pounamu (nephrite) heirlooms, passed down through generations as carriers of ancestral mana.
look: polished nephrite jade cabochon, deep spinach green

name: Rhodolite Garnet
fact: First described from North Carolina's Cowee Valley, its name comes from the Greek for 'rose stone'.
lore: Legend says Noah hung a glowing garnet in the ark to light the way through the dark flood.
look: faceted oval rhodolite garnet, raspberry purple-red

name: Sphalerite
fact: Gem sphalerite has over three times the fire of diamond, but it is far too soft for everyday jewelry.
lore: Old German miners called it 'blende', meaning deceiver, because it looked like lead ore yet yielded no lead.
look: faceted round sphalerite, honey orange with blazing rainbow fire

name: Sugilite
fact: Described in Japan in 1976, sugilite became a gem after vivid purple material turned up in a South African manganese mine.
lore: In modern crystal lore, sugilite is said to be a stone of spiritual love and gentle protection.
look: polished sugilite cabochon, rich magenta purple

name: Ametrine
color: Purple and golden zones in one crystal
fact: Nearly all natural ametrine comes from Bolivia's Anahí mine, where amethyst and citrine zones grew in a single crystal.
lore: Bolivian legend says it reached Europe as a dowry when a conquistador married an Ayoreo princess named Anahí.
look: faceted rectangular ametrine, half purple and half golden yellow

name: Blue Topaz
color: Sky blue to deep London blue
fact: Natural blue topaz is usually pale; most vivid blue topaz sold today is colorless topaz that has been irradiated and heated.
lore: Medieval lapidaries believed topaz could cool tempers and break enchantments when held in the hand.
look: faceted oval blue topaz, bright Swiss blue

name: Brazilianite
fact: First mistaken for chrysoberyl, it was described in 1945 from Minas Gerais and named for its homeland.
lore: Being a modern find, its lore is young: crystal circles embrace it as a cheerful stone of creativity.
look: faceted brazilianite, clear chartreuse yellow-green

name: Chrysoprase
fact: Nickel gives chrysoprase its apple green, making it one of the most valuable chalcedony varieties.
lore: Legend has it that Alexander the Great wore chrysoprase in his girdle to bring victory in battle.
look: polished chrysoprase cabochon, translucent apple green

name: Larimar
fact: Larimar is a blue pectolite found only in the Dominican Republic; its name joins 'Larissa' with mar, Spanish for sea.
lore: Caribbean crystal lore calls larimar the 'Atlantis stone', a modern tradition linking it to the sea.
look: polished larimar cabochon, sea-blue with white wave patterns

name: Mali Garnet
fact: Discovered in Mali in 1994, this grossular–andradite blend pairs grossular's brightness with andradite's fire.
lore: So recently found, it borrows garnet's old tradition as a traveler's protective stone.
look: round brilliant Mali garnet, golden yellow-green with fire

name: Moonstone
color: Colorless to milky white with blue sheen
fact: Its floating glow, called adularescence, comes from light scattering between thin intergrown layers of two feldspars.
lore: Hindu mythology tells that moonstone was formed from moonbeams, and in India it is a traditional lovers' gift.
look: domed moonstone cabochon, milky translucent with floating blue sheen

name: Pyrope Garnet
fact: Bohemian pyrope fueled a 19th-century jewelry craze, and pyropes in kimberlite help prospectors track down diamonds.
lore: Bohemian tradition made pyrope, Greek for 'fiery-eyed', a keepsake of loyalty and lasting friendship.
look: faceted round pyrope garnet, deep blood red

name: Sunstone
color: Peach, orange to red with glittering schiller
fact: Oregon sunstone sparkles from tiny copper platelets, and it became Oregon's state gem in 1987.
lore: A retold Oregon legend says sunstones hold the blood of a wounded warrior, which gave them their red glow.
look: faceted oval Oregon sunstone, peach-red with coppery glitter

name: Almandine Garnet
fact: The most common garnet, almandine was cut into thin plates for Anglo-Saxon cloisonné like the Sutton Hoo treasures.
lore: Medieval Europeans believed garnets glowed in the dark and could guard sleepers against bad dreams.
look: faceted oval almandine garnet, deep wine red

name: Amethyst
fact: Iron traces plus natural irradiation make amethyst purple, and heating can turn it yellow like citrine.
lore: Its name means 'not drunk' in Greek, and ancient Greeks believed amethyst cups guarded against drunkenness.
look: tight cluster of deep purple amethyst points on grey matrix

name: Andalusite
color: Brownish green to orange-brown, changing with angle
fact: Andalusite shares its formula with kyanite and sillimanite; it forms at lower pressure and flashes green and brown.
lore: Its many-sided color play gives it a modern crystal tradition as a stone for seeing all sides of a question.
look: faceted oval andalusite, olive green with orange-brown flashes

name: Charoite
color: Lilac to deep purple with swirling silky fibers
fact: Known from a single region near Siberia's Chara River, charoite was described as a new mineral in 1978.
lore: Modern crystal lore calls charoite a stone of transformation, a tradition as young as the mineral itself.
look: polished charoite cabochon, swirling lilac and violet silky bands

name: Chrome Diopside
fact: Chromium gives it an emerald-like green, but the color is so deep that larger stones can look almost black.
lore: Nicknamed 'Siberian emerald', it is said in crystal folklore to bring vitality and a love of nature.
look: faceted round chrome diopside, intense forest green

name: Danburite
color: Colorless to pale pink or yellow
fact: Named for Danbury, Connecticut, where it was first found in 1839, its crystals resemble topaz.
lore: Crystal tradition holds danburite a stone of serenity, prized for its clear wedge-tipped crystals.
look: clear colorless danburite crystal, sharp wedge-shaped termination

name: Hessonite Garnet
fact: Nicknamed 'cinnamon stone', hessonite has a swirling, syrupy look caused by tiny included crystals.
lore: In Vedic astrology tradition, hessonite (gomed) is the gem of the shadow planet Rahu.
look: faceted oval hessonite garnet, cinnamon orange

name: Iolite
fact: Turn an iolite and it shifts from violet-blue to pale yellow-grey; the gem trade once sold it as 'water sapphire'.
lore: Legend says Viking sailors used thin slices of iolite to find the sun through clouds and fog.
look: faceted cushion iolite, violet-blue

name: Lazulite
fact: Not to be confused with the lazurite in lapis, lazulite forms sharp blue crystals at Yukon's Rapid Creek.
lore: Its name traces to old words for 'heaven', giving it a crystal tradition as a stone of skyward thoughts.
look: sharp deep blue lazulite crystal, glassy and bright

name: Vesuvianite
fact: First described from blocks thrown out by Mount Vesuvius, it is also known as idocrase.
lore: Collectors link vesuvianite to its fiery birthplace, traditionally treating it as a stone of inner strength.
look: faceted oval vesuvianite, olive green with bright luster

name: Apatite
fact: Apatite defines 5 on the Mohs scale, and a form of it is the main mineral in our teeth and bones.
lore: Named from a Greek word for 'deceit' because it mimics other gems, it is linked in crystal lore to motivation.
look: faceted oval neon blue apatite, vivid tropical blue

name: Citrine
fact: Natural citrine is rare; most citrine on the market is heat-treated amethyst that has turned golden.
lore: Nicknamed the 'merchant's stone', citrine is traditionally kept in cash boxes to invite prosperity.
look: faceted cushion citrine, warm golden yellow

name: Goshenite
fact: German 'Brille', eyeglasses, comes from beryl, since some early lenses were ground from clear beryl like goshenite.
lore: Medieval scryers traditionally gazed into polished clear beryl, hoping to glimpse the future.
look: faceted emerald-cut goshenite, water-clear colorless

name: Orthoclase
fact: Orthoclase defines 6 on the Mohs scale; transparent yellow gem orthoclase comes chiefly from Madagascar.
lore: Crystal enthusiasts traditionally link golden orthoclase with sunny optimism and fresh beginnings.
look: faceted oval orthoclase, clear pale golden yellow

name: Scapolite
fact: Scapolite is a series between marialite and meionite; violet cat's-eye stones from Myanmar are a collector favorite.
lore: Crystal folklore calls scapolite a problem-solver's stone, a modern tradition with no ancient source.
look: faceted emerald-cut scapolite, clear golden yellow

name: Cavansite
fact: Its name comes from calcium, vanadium and silicon, and its best rosettes come from quarries near Pune, India.
lore: Crystal lore credits cavansite with lifting creativity, inspired by its startling blue.
look: electric blue cavansite rosettes on white stilbite

name: Dioptase
fact: Kazakh miners once mistook it for emerald; its name means 'to see through', for reflections from inner cleavage.
lore: Its 'Kazakh emerald' history inspires a crystal tradition calling dioptase a stone of the heart.
look: cluster of vivid emerald-green dioptase crystals on matrix

name: Iron Meteorite
color: Metallic grey with etched crosshatch pattern
fact: Etched slices show Widmanstätten patterns, nickel-iron crystals that grew over millions of years of slow cooling.
lore: Ancient Egyptians called iron 'metal of heaven', and Tutankhamun's dagger was forged from meteoritic iron.
look: etched iron meteorite slice with metallic Widmanstätten crosshatch

name: Moldavite
formula: Silica-rich glass from a meteorite impact
fact: Moldavite formed about 15 million years ago when a meteorite struck Germany's Ries crater, flinging molten glass into Bohemia.
lore: Modern crystal lore holds moldavite to be a powerful 'stone of transformation' from the stars.
look: raw moldavite fragment, translucent forest green with sculpted pitted surface

name: Native Silver
fact: Norway's Kongsberg mines produced famous wire silver, curling strands that grow like hair from the rock.
lore: European folklore credits silver with warding off werewolves and evil spirits, as in silver bullet tales.
look: curling native wire silver specimen, bright silvery strands

name: Crocoite
fact: Chromium, now vital to stainless steel, was discovered in 1797 by analyzing crocoite from Siberia.
lore: Tasmanians honor crocoite as their island's mineral emblem, a cherished tradition since 2000.
look: spray of bright orange-red crocoite needle crystals

name: Fire Agate
formula: SiO₂ with layers of iron oxide
color: Brown with iridescent orange, green and gold flashes
fact: Thin layers of iron oxide within the chalcedony diffract light into rainbow fire just below the surface.
lore: Crystal folklore says fire agate holds the spirit of flame, a traditional stone of courage.
look: polished fire agate cabochon, brown with iridescent orange-green fire

name: Libyan Desert Glass
fact: Formed about 29 million years ago, possibly by a meteorite airburst, this glass is roughly 98% silica.
lore: A scarab of it sits in Tutankhamun's pectoral, giving it a tradition as a sacred solar stone of Egypt.
look: raw translucent pale golden Libyan desert glass, wind-polished

name: Rhodochrosite
color: Rose pink to cherry red, often banded
fact: Colorado's Sweet Home Mine produced world-famous cherry-red rhombs, and rhodochrosite is Colorado's state mineral.
lore: Argentine legend calls it 'Inca rose', saying it formed from the blood of ancient Inca rulers.
look: polished banded rhodochrosite slice, rose pink and white rings

name: Blue John
fact: Found only near Castleton in Derbyshire, it has been carved into vases and bowls since the 18th century.
lore: Local tradition says the name comes from French 'bleu-jaune', blue-yellow, though the origin is debated.
look: polished Blue John fluorite, banded purple-blue and honey yellow

name: Cuprite
fact: Namibia's Onganja mine yielded cuprite crystals large and clean enough to facet into rare deep red gems.
lore: Crystal lore links cuprite's copper red to vitality and the steady warmth of the hearth.
look: dark crimson cuprite octahedral crystal with metallic red glints

name: Wulfenite
color: Orange, yellow to red tabular plates
origin: Red Cloud Mine, Arizona (USA), Mexico, Slovenia
fact: Arizona's Red Cloud Mine is famed for blood-red square plates, and wulfenite is Arizona's state mineral.
lore: Crystal folklore links wulfenite's glowing thin plates to creativity and manifesting ideas.
look: thin tabular orange-red wulfenite plates on matrix

name: Adamite
color: Lime green to yellow, glowing under UV
fact: Mexico's Ojuela Mine yields lime-green adamite sprays that glow bright green under ultraviolet light.
lore: Crystal folklore names adamite a stone of joy, inspired by its cheerful glowing green.
look: spray of lime-green adamite crystals on brown limonite

name: Azurite
fact: Azurite slowly alters to green malachite, and pigment ground from it colored many medieval paintings.
lore: Crystal folklore names azurite a 'stone of heaven', said to awaken insight.
look: cluster of deep azure blue azurite crystals

name: Cobaltoan Calcite
fact: Traces of cobalt give this calcite its vivid hot pink, often as sparkling crusts in Congo's copper mines.
lore: Crystal tradition makes it a heart stone of self-forgiveness, inspired by its bright pink.
look: sparkling druzy hot-pink cobaltoan calcite on dark matrix

name: Hackmanite
color: Pale pink to violet; shifts after UV and light
fact: This sulfur-bearing sodalite is tenebrescent, changing color after UV exposure and fading back in daylight.
lore: Crystal enthusiasts traditionally call hackmanite a 'chameleon stone' tied to adaptability.
look: raw hackmanite chunk, raspberry violet fading to white

name: Herkimer Diamond
fact: Not diamonds at all, these double-pointed quartz crystals grew in cavities of dolostone about 500 million years old.
lore: Crystal tradition calls Herkimers 'attunement stones', prized for their naturally faceted double points.
look: small double-terminated water-clear Herkimer diamond quartz crystal

name: Mimetite
fact: Its name, from the Greek for 'imitator', reflects how closely it resembles pyromorphite.
lore: Playing on its imitator name, crystal tradition ties mimetite to finding one's own path.
look: cluster of bright yellow-orange mimetite barrel crystals

name: Pietersite
color: Swirling blue, gold and brown shimmer
fact: Described by Sid Pieters in 1962 from Namibia, it is a brecciated tiger's eye whose fibers were folded into swirls.
lore: Crystal lore calls pietersite the 'tempest stone', its swirling shimmer read as storms of insight.
look: polished pietersite with swirling blue and gold chatoyance

name: Rutilated Quartz
color: Clear with golden to reddish needles
fact: The golden 'hairs' are rutile crystals that formed first and were later engulfed by the growing quartz.
lore: Old European tradition called it 'Venus hair stone', imagining the needles as the goddess's golden locks.
look: polished clear quartz with dense golden rutile needles

name: Smithsonite
origin: Kelly Mine, New Mexico (USA), Tsumeb (Namibia), Mexico
fact: Named for James Smithson, founder of the Smithsonian; its pearly crusts come in pink, blue and green.
lore: Crystal tradition calls smithsonite a gentle 'kindness stone', a modern association with its soft colors.
look: botryoidal pastel blue-green smithsonite with pearly luster

name: Stibnite
fact: Japan's Ichinokawa mine produced sword-like stibnite crystals up to about 60 cm long.
lore: Kohl made from stibnite lined ancient Egyptian eyes, worn by tradition to ward off the evil eye.
look: spray of metallic silver-grey stibnite blades

name: Uvarovite
fact: The rarest of the common garnets, uvarovite forms sparkling druzes of crystals usually too small to facet.
lore: Named for a Russian count, it is gifted in crystal circles as a stone of abundance.
look: sparkling emerald-green uvarovite garnet druzy on dark matrix

name: Vanadinite
fact: Morocco's Mibladen mines produce glossy red hexagonal crystals, and vanadinite is an ore of vanadium.
lore: Crystal circles traditionally treat vanadinite as a stone of stamina, inspired by its fiery red.
look: cluster of glossy red hexagonal vanadinite crystals on matrix

name: Amber
origin: Baltic Sea coast, Dominican Republic, Myanmar
fact: Baltic amber is tens of millions of years old and can preserve insects and plant fragments in perfect detail.
lore: Greek myth says amber formed from the tears of the Heliades, mourning their brother Phaethon.
look: polished honey-orange amber nugget, glowing translucent

name: Covellite
fact: Covellite was the first known natural superconductor, though only at temperatures near absolute zero.
lore: Crystal folklore calls covellite a 'dream stone', its indigo said to deepen reflection.
look: indigo blue covellite plates with purple iridescent flash

name: Lake Superior Agate
color: Red, orange and white iron-stained bands
fact: Born in lava flows about 1.1 billion years old, these agates were spread by glaciers across the upper Midwest.
lore: Minnesota made it the state gemstone in 1969, and beachcomber lore treats a first find as a sign of luck.
look: polished Lake Superior agate, red and orange concentric bands

name: Native Copper
color: Copper red, tarnishing brown or green
fact: Michigan's Keweenaw Peninsula held enormous masses of native copper, one weighing hundreds of tonnes.
lore: Copper's ancient link to Venus and Cyprus gave it a lasting tradition as the metal of love.
look: branching native copper specimen, coppery red with dendritic arms

name: Ocean Jasper
color: Green, white and pink orb patterns
fact: Its orbs are radiating chalcedony spheres, and the classic coastal deposit can be reached only at low tide.
lore: Madagascar's seashore gave it a modern crystal tradition as a stone of joy and patience.
look: polished ocean jasper with green and pink orbicular eyes

name: Pyromorphite
color: Grass green to yellow, barrel-shaped prisms
fact: Its name means 'fire form': a melted bead of it recrystallizes into crystal faces as it cools.
lore: Collectors traditionally link pyromorphite's green to garden growth, calling it a nature stone.
look: cluster of grass-green barrel-shaped pyromorphite crystals

name: Rainbow Moonstone
color: Milky white with blue and rainbow sheen
fact: Despite the name, it is a white labradorite, not true moonstone, which is a potassium feldspar.
lore: Indian tradition pairs it with moonstone as a lunar gem, a customary token of love.
look: polished rainbow moonstone, milky white with blue rainbow flash

name: Seraphinite
color: Dark green with silvery feathery shimmer
fact: This Siberian clinochlore shows silvery, feather-like flashes as its mica-like flakes catch the light.
lore: Named for the six-winged seraphim, it is traditionally linked to angelic guardianship.
look: polished seraphinite, dark green with silvery feather patterns

name: Agatized Coral
color: Cream, pink and tan with flower-like polyp patterns
fact: Ancient coral colonies were replaced by chalcedony, and Florida made agatized coral its state stone in 1979.
lore: Collectors traditionally call its fossil polyp rosettes 'flowers of the sea'.
look: polished agatized coral with cream flower-like polyp patterns

name: Apophyllite
fact: Its name means 'to flake off' in Greek, as it peels into thin layers when heated.
lore: Crystal lore regards apophyllite pyramids as tools for meditation and mental clarity.
look: cluster of glassy colorless apophyllite pyramids

name: Blue Chalcedony
fact: Chalcedony is quartz made of fibers too small to see, and its soft blue comes largely from scattered light.
lore: In crystal folklore, blue chalcedony is said to soothe nerves and encourage gentle speech.
look: tumbled translucent lavender-blue chalcedony

name: Blue Lace Agate
color: Pale blue with white lacy bands
fact: Classic blue lace agate came from a single deposit in southern Namibia, making old material a collector favorite.
lore: Crystal tradition calls it a throat stone, said to help shy speakers find their voice.
look: polished blue lace agate, pale sky blue with white lace banding

name: Celestite
fact: Celestite is a main source of strontium, and Ohio's Crystal Cave formed inside a giant celestite geode.
lore: Named from Latin 'caelestis', heavenly, it is linked in crystal tradition to angelic realms.
look: geode cluster of pale sky-blue celestite crystals

name: Hemimorphite
color: Sky blue to white, botryoidal or bladed
fact: Its name means 'half shape': the two ends of each crystal differ, a sign of its polar structure.
lore: Crystal folklore says hemimorphite encourages self-reflection, honoring its two-faced crystals.
look: botryoidal sky-blue hemimorphite with soft silky luster

name: Jet
fact: Whitby jet formed from Jurassic trees related to the monkey puzzle and boomed as Victorian mourning jewelry.
lore: Queen Victoria wore jet while mourning Albert, and older folk tradition hung it in homes to ward off evil.
look: polished jet cabochon, deep velvety black

name: Labradorite
color: Grey to dark with blue, green and gold flash
fact: Its flash, called labradorescence, comes from light interfering in microscopic layers inside the feldspar.
lore: Inuit legend tells that the northern lights were trapped in Labrador's rocks until a warrior freed most with his spear.
look: polished labradorite slab with blue-green flash

name: Malachite
fact: Ural malachite clad whole palace rooms in St. Petersburg, including the Malachite Room of the Winter Palace.
lore: In crystal folklore, malachite is said to be a stone of transformation and a protector of travelers.
look: polished malachite with bands of light and dark green

name: Nuummite
fact: Found near Nuuk, Greenland, this metamorphic rock is around 3 billion years old and flashes gold from amphibole fibers.
lore: Crystal lore calls nuummite the 'sorcerer's stone', a modern name for an ancient rock.
look: polished black nuummite with golden iridescent flashes

name: Pink Opal
fact: Unlike precious opal, Peruvian pink opal is common opal with no play-of-color, valued for its soft solid pink.
lore: Crystal folklore calls pink opal a gentle heart stone, said to soothe old hurts.
look: tumbled soft pink Peruvian opal, waxy and opaque

name: Rainbow Obsidian
fact: Its rainbow bands appear when light strikes layers of tiny aligned mineral crystals within the glass.
lore: Some crystal lore calls rainbow obsidian a gentle stone, hiding cheer beneath a dark surface.
look: polished rainbow obsidian, black with purple-green iridescent bands

name: Ruby in Zoisite
formula: Rock: green zoisite with ruby (corundum) and hornblende
fact: Called anyolite, from a Maasai word for green, it pairs opaque ruby crystals with green zoisite and black hornblende.
lore: Crystal folklore says ruby in zoisite unites passion with patience, a modern pairing of its two colors.
look: polished ruby in zoisite, green with pinkish-red ruby crystals and black flecks

name: Tourmalinated Quartz
fact: Black needles of schorl tourmaline cut through the quartz, trapped as the host crystal grew around them.
lore: Crystal folklore says it unites quartz's clarity with tourmaline's grounding, two stones in one.
look: polished clear quartz crossed by black tourmaline needles

name: Variscite
color: Apple to bluish green with brown veins
fact: Utah variscite is sometimes mistaken for turquoise, but it is an aluminum phosphate with no copper.
lore: Crystal circles traditionally treat variscite as a worry stone, rubbed smooth for calm.
look: polished variscite, apple green with brown spiderweb veins

name: Amazonite
fact: Traces of lead and water in microcline give amazonite its color; no deposits are known along the Amazon.
lore: Legend links it to the warrior Amazons, said to adorn their shields with the stone.
look: tumbled amazonite, blue-green with white streaks

name: Angelite
fact: Angelite is a blue anhydrite, gypsum without its water, and it can slowly turn back to gypsum in damp air.
lore: Its lore is recent: crystal circles adopted it in the late 20th century as a stone of calm and connection.
look: tumbled pale lavender-blue angelite, soft matte sheen

name: Barite
fact: Barite is surprisingly heavy for a pale mineral; its name comes from the Greek 'barys', heavy.
lore: Oklahoma made barite roses its state rock, and local tradition gives them as rustic keepsakes.
look: cluster of golden tabular barite blades

name: Bismuth
color: Silvery pink-white; rainbow oxide on lab crystals
fact: The stepped rainbow 'hopper' crystals sold widely are lab-grown from melted bismuth; their colors are a thin oxide film.
lore: Saxon miners called it 'wismut', and modern crystal lore links its staircase shapes to change.
look: lab-grown iridescent bismuth hopper crystal, stepped rainbow staircase

name: Bloodstone
fact: Also called heliotrope, bloodstone is green chalcedony speckled with red spots of iron oxide.
lore: Medieval Christian legend held that its red spots were drops of Christ's blood fallen on green stone.
look: tumbled dark green bloodstone with red speckles

name: Botswana Agate
color: Fine grey, pink and peach bands
fact: Formed in gas pockets of ancient basalt, its delicate pink-grey banding can run to hundreds of fine layers.
lore: In crystal folklore Botswana agate is a 'sunset stone', said to steady you through times of change.
look: polished Botswana agate with fine pink and grey banding

name: Chrysanthemum Stone
formula: Rock: celestite or calcite 'flowers' in limestone
color: White flower patterns on dark grey rock
fact: Its white petals are radiating crystals, originally celestite often replaced by calcite, grown in dark limestone.
lore: In China and Japan it is traditionally prized as a stone of good fortune, its blossoms evoking the chrysanthemum.
look: polished chrysanthemum stone, white flower patterns on dark grey

name: Chrysocolla
fact: A soft copper silicate, chrysocolla's name means 'gold glue', after an ancient solder used for gold.
lore: Crystal tradition links chrysocolla to calm communication and the peaceful energy of water.
look: polished chrysocolla, mottled turquoise blue and green

name: Crazy Lace Agate
color: Cream, red, gold and grey swirling bands
fact: Found in northern Mexico, its tightly folded, chaotic banding is also sold as 'Mexican lace agate'.
lore: Nicknamed the 'laughter stone', it is traditionally said to lift the spirit.
look: polished crazy lace agate with swirling cream and red bands

name: Dendritic Agate
color: Milky white with black fern-like dendrites
fact: Its fern-like patterns are manganese oxide crystals that branched along tiny cracks; they are not fossils.
lore: Victorian collectors cherished it as 'tree stone', a keepsake said to hold tiny forests sealed inside.
look: polished dendritic agate, milky white with black fern-like branches

name: Epidote
fact: Austria's Knappenwand produced dark green epidote crystals widely regarded as the world's finest.
lore: Crystal lore links pistachio-green epidote to growth and the gathering of strength.
look: spray of glossy dark green striated epidote crystals

name: Hawk's Eye
fact: Hawk's eye is tiger's eye before oxidation: its blue-grey crocidolite fibers never altered to brown iron oxide.
lore: Folk tradition names it for the far-seeing hawk, a stone said to sharpen perspective.
look: polished blue-grey hawk's eye with silky chatoyant bands

name: Iceland Spar
fact: Iceland spar's strong double refraction doubles any image seen through it, and it helped reveal polarized light.
lore: Norse sagas mention a 'sunstone' for finding the sun in clouds, and tradition says it was Iceland spar.
look: water-clear Iceland spar calcite rhomb

name: Kyanite
color: Blue blades, also green or black
fact: Kyanite's hardness changes with direction: a knife scratches it along the blade but not across it.
lore: A modern crystal belief holds that kyanite never needs cleansing, calling it 'self-clearing'.
look: bladed blue kyanite cluster with pearly streaks

name: Okenite
fact: Okenite forms soft, fur-like 'cotton balls' of hair-thin fibers in the gas pockets of Indian basalt.
lore: Named for naturalist Lorenz Oken, its snowball tufts are treated in crystal lore as stones of comfort.
look: fluffy white okenite cotton-ball puffs in a basalt pocket

name: Petoskey Stone
fact: These fossil Hexagonaria corals lived in Devonian seas about 350 million years ago; they are Michigan's state stone.
lore: Michigan legend links the stone's name to Chief Petosegay, whose name is said to mean 'rising sun'.
look: polished grey Petoskey stone with hexagonal fossil coral pattern

name: Petrified Wood
color: Brown, red, grey with wood grain
fact: Silica-rich water replaced wood cell by cell; logs in Arizona's Petrified Forest are over 200 million years old.
lore: A retold Navajo story says the stone logs are the bones of a giant slain long ago.
look: polished petrified wood round showing tree rings in red and brown

name: Polychrome Jasper
color: Red, brown, cream and mustard swirls
fact: Found in Madagascar in the 2000s, its swirling desert colors come from iron oxides in the silica.
lore: Called 'desert jasper', it is linked in crystal circles to creativity and warmth.
look: polished polychrome jasper, swirling red, cream and mustard bands

name: Prehnite
fact: Named in 1788 for Dutch colonel Hendrik von Prehn, it is often cited as the first mineral named after a person.
lore: Crystal folklore calls prehnite a 'stone of prophecy', traditionally used to quiet the mind.
look: botryoidal pale green prehnite with dark epidote needles

name: Scolecite
fact: A zeolite from India's basalts, its name comes from the Greek for 'worm': heated, it curls like one.
lore: Crystal tradition counts scolecite among calming stones, its radiating needles said to settle a busy mind.
look: radiating spray of slender white scolecite needles

name: Septarian Nodule
formula: Rock: clay-rich concretion with calcite and aragonite
fact: Formed in seafloor mud millions of years ago, these nodules cracked and filled with yellow calcite in starry patterns.
lore: Also called 'dragon stone', septarian is said in crystal folklore to foster patience and calm speech.
look: polished septarian nodule half with yellow calcite star veins

name: Smoky Quartz
fact: Smoky quartz gets its color from natural radiation acting on traces of aluminum in the crystal.
lore: Scottish tradition prizes smoky 'cairngorm' quartz, set in kilt pins and dirk handles as Highland talismans.
look: tall smoky quartz point, translucent smoky brown

name: Staurolite
fact: Its twin crystals cross at 60° or 90° to form natural X's and crosses; it is Georgia's state mineral.
lore: Virginia legend says these 'fairy crosses' formed from fairies' tears on hearing of Christ's death.
look: brown staurolite twin crystal forming a natural cross

name: Sulfur
fact: Native sulfur forms around volcanic vents, and its crystals can crack from the warmth of a hand.
lore: Called 'brimstone' in old texts, it was traditionally burned to drive away evil and disease.
look: cluster of bright lemon-yellow sulfur crystals

name: Thunder Egg
formula: Rock: rhyolite shell with agate or chalcedony core
color: Brown shell with agate star core
fact: These rhyolite nodules hide star-shaped cores of agate, and Oregon named the thunder egg its state rock in 1965.
lore: A retold Native American legend says thunder spirits hurled the eggs at one another in anger.
look: cut and polished thunder egg half, brown shell around blue agate star

name: Tiger Iron
formula: Rock: tiger's eye, red jasper and hematite
color: Banded gold, red and metallic grey
fact: A banded iron formation over 2 billion years old, its layers record ancient seas as oxygen built up on Earth.
lore: Crystal folklore calls tiger iron a stone of stamina, three stones in one.
look: polished tiger iron slab, bands of gold, red jasper and silver hematite

name: Turritella Agate
color: Dark brown with white spiral shell sections
fact: Despite the name, its fossils are freshwater Elimia snails, not marine Turritella, from Wyoming's Green River Formation.
lore: Fossil stones like this are traditionally kept by collectors as links to ancient life and deep time.
look: polished turritella agate, dark brown packed with white spiral snail fossils

name: Aragonite
color: Orange-brown, white or blue; star-like clusters
fact: Aragonite shares calcite's formula but not its structure, and mollusks build shells and pearls from it.
lore: Named for Spain's Aragón, its starry 'sputnik' clusters are kept as grounding stones in crystal tradition.
look: starburst sputnik cluster of orange-brown aragonite

name: Black Tourmaline
fact: Schorl is the most common tourmaline; its long, striated prisms have a rounded triangular cross section.
lore: Crystal lore holds black tourmaline as a protective stone, traditionally placed by doorways.
look: raw striated black tourmaline prism, glossy jet black

name: Bornite
fact: Fresh bornite is bronze, but it quickly tarnishes purple and blue, earning the nickname 'peacock ore'.
lore: Crystal folklore calls bornite a 'happiness stone', inspired by its peacock colors.
look: raw bornite chunk with iridescent purple and blue peacock tarnish

name: Carnelian
fact: Iron oxide colors carnelian; Indus Valley artisans drilled and etched carnelian beads over 4,000 years ago.
lore: Ancient Egyptians placed carnelian amulets with the dead, meant to ease the journey to the afterlife.
look: tumbled translucent orange carnelian, glowing like an ember

name: Chalcopyrite
fact: The most important copper ore, it is softer and yellower than pyrite and tarnishes to iridescent blues and purples.
lore: Alchemists saw its brassy sheen as a hint of hidden gold, another 'fool's gold' of old tradition.
look: brassy golden chalcopyrite crystals with iridescent tarnish

name: Chiastolite
color: Grey-brown with a dark cross pattern
fact: Carbonaceous inclusions in andalusite crystals line up as a dark cross, seen when a crystal is sliced across.
lore: Tradition says pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela carried chiastolite crosses as protective tokens.
look: polished chiastolite cross-section showing a dark cross

name: Clear Quartz
fact: Quartz is piezoelectric: squeezed, it produces a voltage, which is why quartz crystals keep time in watches.
lore: Ancient Greeks thought clear quartz was ice frozen so hard it could never thaw; krystallos means ice.
look: cluster of water-clear quartz points with sharp terminations

name: Desert Rose
fact: These rosettes form as gypsum crystallizes in damp desert sand, trapping grains between its bladed petals.
lore: In crystal folklore, desert rose helps one let go of old patterns, as the sand shapes the petals.
look: sandy tan gypsum desert rose rosette with bladed petals

name: Fluorite
color: Purple, green, blue, yellow, often banded
fact: Fluorite gave its name to fluorescence, and many specimens glow blue-violet under ultraviolet light.
lore: Some crystal circles call fluorite the 'genius stone', a tradition linking it to order and focus.
look: translucent purple and green banded fluorite octahedron

name: Galena
fact: The chief ore of lead, galena breaks into perfect cubes and served as the detector in early 'crystal' radios.
lore: Alchemical tradition tied lead to Saturn, and crystal lore now calls galena a grounding stone.
look: cluster of bright silvery galena cubes

name: Larvikite
fact: This Norwegian igneous rock, Norway's national stone, is polished worldwide for building facades.
lore: Crystal folklore nicknames it 'Norwegian moonstone', a stone traditionally tied to intuition.
look: polished larvikite, dark grey with silvery-blue feldspar flashes

name: Lepidolite
fact: A lithium-rich mica, lepidolite is an ore of lithium, and its name means 'scale stone' in Greek.
lore: Crystal folklore calls lepidolite a 'peace stone', traditionally kept close in stressful times.
look: tumbled lilac lepidolite with glittering mica flakes

name: Lodestone
fact: Lodestone is naturally magnetized magnetite, possibly by lightning; early compasses used it to find north.
lore: Ancient lore tells of the shepherd Magnes, whose iron-nailed sandals stuck to a lodestone on Mount Ida.
look: raw black lodestone with tiny iron filings clinging to it

name: Mookaite
color: Mustard yellow, red, purple and cream
fact: A silicified radiolarite, mookaite is built from the microscopic shells of ancient marine plankton.
lore: Named for Mooka Creek, it carries a modern crystal tradition as a stone of adventure.
look: tumbled mookaite, mottled mustard, red and purple

name: Moss Agate
color: Clear to milky with green moss-like inclusions
fact: The 'moss' is not plant life but branching inclusions of green chlorite or iron and manganese minerals.
lore: Long known as the gardener's stone, folk tradition says moss agate brings good harvests.
look: tumbled moss agate, translucent with green moss-like inclusions

name: Picture Jasper
color: Tan and brown with landscape-like patterns
fact: Silica-rich mud and volcanic ash hardened into scenes of hills and skies, prized for 'landscape' cabochons.
lore: Folk tradition calls picture jasper Earth's storybook, a stone for remembering the past.
look: polished picture jasper slab with brown desert landscape patterns

name: Pyrite
fact: Spain's Navajún mines yield near-perfect natural cubes; 'fool's gold' throws sparks when struck against steel.
lore: Its name means 'fire' in Greek, and modern folk tradition keeps pyrite on desks as a stone of abundance.
look: cluster of sharp brassy gold pyrite cubes

name: Rhodonite
color: Pink to rose red with black veins
fact: Its name comes from the Greek 'rhodon', rose; Ural rhodonite was carved for the Russian imperial court.
lore: Crystal lore calls rhodonite a 'rescue stone', said to bring calm in emotional storms.
look: tumbled pink rhodonite with black manganese veins

name: Rose Quartz
fact: Rose quartz is usually massive; its pink is linked to microscopic fibers of a dumortierite-like mineral.
lore: Crystal folklore names rose quartz the stone of unconditional love, tied in retellings to Aphrodite.
look: tumbled pink rose quartz, milky translucent

name: Shungite
formula: Rock: largely noncrystalline carbon with silicates
fact: Found near Lake Onega in Karelia, this carbon-rich rock is about 2 billion years old.
lore: Karelian tradition credits Peter the Great with founding a spa at nearby springs to refresh his soldiers.
look: raw glossy black shungite chunk with silvery sheen

name: Stilbite
fact: Stilbite grows in wheat-sheaf or bow-tie bundles inside gas pockets of India's Deccan basalt.
lore: Crystal folklore regards stilbite as a gentle travel stone, said to ease the journey.
look: peach stilbite bow-tie sheaf crystals with pearly luster

name: Tiger's Eye
formula: SiO₂ with altered crocidolite fibers and iron oxides
color: Golden brown with silky shifting bands
fact: Its rolling silky shine comes from quartz grown around fine, parallel crocidolite fibers altered to iron oxides.
lore: Roman soldiers are said to have carried engraved tiger's eye for courage and protection in battle.
look: tumbled golden-brown tiger's eye with silky chatoyant bands

name: Apache Tears
fact: These small obsidian nodules weather out of perlite; held up to light, they glow translucent smoky brown.
lore: Legend tells that the tears of Apache women mourning fallen warriors turned to stone where they fell.
look: small rounded Apache tear obsidian nodule, translucent smoky black

name: Fuchsite
fact: Chromium turns this muscovite mica green, and it is the glitter inside green aventurine.
lore: Crystal tradition names fuchsite a 'healer's helper', a modern folk belief tied to its green glow.
look: raw sparkly emerald-green fuchsite mica chunk

name: Green Aventurine
color: Light to medium green with glittery spangles
fact: Its shimmer, called aventurescence, comes from tiny flakes of green chromium-bearing mica.
lore: Nicknamed the 'gambler's stone', green aventurine is traditionally carried for luck in games of chance.
look: tumbled green aventurine, soft green with subtle glitter

name: Hematite
fact: Polished hematite looks silver-black, yet it leaves a blood-red streak; its name comes from the Greek for blood.
lore: Legend says Roman soldiers rubbed hematite on their bodies, believing it made them invincible.
look: tumbled hematite, metallic silver-black mirror shine

name: Howlite
color: White with grey to black web veins
fact: Porous howlite takes dye easily and is often dyed blue to imitate turquoise.
lore: Crystal folklore holds howlite a calming stone, traditionally tucked under pillows for restful sleep.
look: tumbled white howlite with fine grey web veining

name: Obsidian
fact: Obsidian forms when lava cools too fast to crystallize; a freshly fractured edge can be sharper than a steel scalpel.
lore: Aztec priests polished obsidian into mirrors, a tradition tied to the god Tezcatlipoca, 'Smoking Mirror'.
look: polished black obsidian, glossy mirror-like surface

name: Onyx
fact: True onyx is banded chalcedony; much 'black onyx' sold today is chalcedony dyed with a sugar-and-acid treatment.
lore: From the Greek for fingernail, legend says Cupid trimmed sleeping Venus's nails and the gods turned them to stone.
look: polished banded black and white onyx

name: Orange Calcite
fact: Calcite fizzes in weak acid and defines 3 on the Mohs scale; traces of iron give this variety its orange.
lore: Crystal folklore calls orange calcite a stone of creative spark and playful energy.
look: raw orange calcite chunk, waxy translucent tangerine

name: Red Jasper
fact: Jasper is opaque microcrystalline quartz packed with impurities; hematite gives red jasper its color.
lore: Ancient Egyptians carved red jasper into the tyet amulet, associated with the goddess Isis.
look: tumbled brick-red jasper, smooth and opaque

name: Selenite
fact: Mexico's Naica Cave of the Crystals holds selenite beams over 11 m long, among the largest crystals known.
lore: Named for Selene, the Greek moon goddess, it is traditionally kept as a cleansing 'moon stone'.
look: satiny white selenite wand with silky fibrous luster

name: Serpentine
fact: Named for its snakeskin-like mottling, serpentine forms when olivine-rich rock reacts with water underground.
lore: Medieval lore held that serpentine protected its bearer from snakebite and poison.
look: tumbled mottled green serpentine, waxy luster

name: Snowflake Obsidian
fact: The snowflakes are radial clusters of cristobalite, a form of silica that grew as the glass slowly devitrified.
lore: Crystal tradition calls it a stone of balance, its pale flakes like light in darkness.
look: tumbled snowflake obsidian, black with white starburst flakes

name: Sodalite
fact: Often mistaken for lapis, sodalite seldom holds pyrite and usually shows white veins of other minerals.
lore: Crystal tradition calls sodalite a 'poet's stone', said to unite logic and expression.
look: tumbled royal blue sodalite with white veins

name: Unakite
formula: Rock: pink feldspar, green epidote, quartz
fact: Named for the Unaka Mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee, unakite is granite altered by epidote.
lore: Crystal tradition calls unakite a stone of partnership, its pink and green growing together.
look: tumbled unakite, mottled salmon pink and olive green
